articles.title: How this Vancouver artist helped bring Canada to life in Marvel's Wolverine
articles.text:
It’s rare for Canada to play itself in games. It’s even rarer for Canada to play itself in big-budget games.
That’s why Canadians were excited to see North Vancouver featured so prominently in gameplay footage from the next PlayStation blockbuster, developer Insomniac Games’ Marvel’s Wolverine. Not only does it give an oft-unseen representation of Canada in gaming, but it also pays tribute to Wolverine’s Canadian roots. (It’s also not the only Canadian location players will visit, as creative director Marcus Smith teased to us.)
And while Insomniac is based in Burbank, California, a veteran Canadian artist has been spearheading the studio’s Canadian representation in Marvel’s Wolverine. Enter Gavin Goulden, senior art director who’s worked on the likes of Irrational’s BioShock Infinite and Insomniac’s Sunset Overdrive and Marvel’s Spider-Man series. The Halifax native now lives in Vancouver, giving him a particularly strong personal connection to ol’ Canucklehead’s latest gaming adventure.
MobileSyrup sat down with Goulden to learn more about the journey to bring Canada to life in Marvel’s Wolverine, the differences of working on Spider-Man vs. Wolverine, how his art has evolved across several games and the advancement of technology, and more.
For people who might not be aware, what does your job as senior art director entail? What does that work look like on a day-to-day basis for Marvel’s Wolverine?
Gavin Goulden: My day-to-day work is really focusing on the team to make sure that we have a consistent visual style on the project. So part of that is fulfilling the player fantasy and having that in every aspect of the game. But it’s also working with a team of leads and a team of artists to make sure that we’re delivering the highest quality we possibly can.
With Marvel’s Wolverine, a lot of people are really excited because this is a Canadian character, and we get to finally see him in Canadian locations in a game of this scale. But we don’t often see that in media. It’s alluded to sometimes, like in X-Men: Origins Wolverine, there’s that fun bit, “Serve your country!” “I’m Canadian.” Or even in Deadpool and Wolverine, we see the CN Tower behind them. But Marvel’s Wolverine is the biggest example of this kind of Canadian representation. So where did that inspiration come from? How did those whole discussions begin in terms of bringing Canada into the game?
Goulden: As everyone knows, Wolverine is Canadian — possibly the most famous Canadian superhero there is, though Wolverine will never call himself a hero. But we felt it was really important to have him in his home country. So when we picked Vancouver, it’s a little different than what comic fans might be used to, but we also knew that we could do Canada justice because Canada rarely gets to play itself. Vancouver, especially, doesn’t get to play itself, so usually it’ll be New York or something like that. But it’s very rare that Vancouver is Vancouver, and being able to represent that was extremely important.
And honestly, it was a cool opportunity to be able to give a place that I love justice. We did a lot of research. It’s kind of in my backyard, so it’s not a ton of research I need to do, but wanting to show like the sulphur pile, which is an iconic landmark in Vancouver… It also gave us room to have a fantastical version of Vancouver, too. And then also, as you’ve seen, getting the Squamish signs, the Sea-to-Sky Highway, and having that be a familiar yet cool Marvel experience, too.
Once you decided that Vancouver would be featured in the game, how did you decide on those specific elements, like the sulphur piles, to include?
Goulden: It was essentially, “How can we place Wolverine in a location that would support the more brutal combat?” So not wanting to be downtown and slicing through a bunch of people and causing chaos in that way. But it’s also a good segue, as you saw in the gameplay trailer, of going from a location to a motorcycle ride. So that location geographically fit the gameplay beats that we wanted to set up.
As someone who is actually not only Canadian but living in Vancouver now, what are you hoping to convey about the city or Canadiana as a whole to players? Especially Marvel fans who aren’t from Canada or aren’t familiar with Vancouver.
Goulden: Wanting to pay respect to a very beautiful location in the world. Part of it’s also breaking a stereotype. Again, since you rarely get to see the city itself or the location itself. So getting to see the authentic version of it might help maybe inspire people to come pay a visit. You can even do that drive in real life. I do it all the time. So hopefully, [we’ll] get some people in to see how beautiful it is in real life.
Is there anything that you were particularly jazzed about getting to include?
Goulden: The wording on the signage, driving up the Sea-to-Sky Highway, is very authentic to British Columbia. Since the Olympics when we added the Squamish translations of the words. So having that small detail, if people can pick up on that, I feel super happy about it. It’s a very, very specific detail that is important to me.
Looking at your job as a whole… A lot of people are very excited when they see authentic, hand-drawn art nowadays — they really respond to that human touch. What goes into making good art direction?
Goulden: A lot of it is conveying the emotion and the gameplay beats that you want in the game. So art really serves gameplay in that way, and trying to sell how you’re intended to feel in cinematics and when you’re in the fight. So in order to make that happen, we do a lot of pre-planning, a lot of concept work, colour scripts, mood boards, stuff like that, to get people all on the same page. That’s really the main thing: getting everybody looking at the same thing and wanting the same goal. So throughout the project, you have to hit all those beats, then also make sure that everything’s consistent so that one mission doesn’t look wildly different from the other and that it’s a very balanced, cohesive feeling project.
Insomniac has made three Spider-Man games now, and Wolverine inhabits the same universe, but obviously, it’s in its own pocket of it. When you’re coming into Wolverine, how did you want to differentiate that from Spider-Man, which is a similar sort of photorealistic visual style, but obviously Wolverine’s more of a gritty character. How did you go about approaching making Wolverine feel similar and something that could realistically co-exist with Spider-Man, but also be its own distinct thing?
Goulden: Totally. While they share the same universe, 1048, and they are kind of based in the same world, so to speak, Wolverine is a much more gritty, brutal, violent character. The world he belongs in is violent, and he’s a violent weapon, so to speak. So that contrast between him and Spider-Man was super important. I’d also say that Spider-Man is my childhood hero, but Wolverine is the hero of my adolescence. So being able to kind of translate that in my career has been a really cool experience. Because you’re going from the “Friendly Neighbourhood Spider-Man” to the living weapon of Wolverine. And I think we showed that difference through brutal combat, being very ferocious and stuff like that is super important and a great opportunity between the two.
I imagine as an artist, as a game developer, working on these beloved Marvel characters is a little bit of a double-edged sword in the sense that on the one hand they’re very beloved, and it must be an honour to work on that. But then there’s a lot of pressure that comes with decades and decades of lore and fandom behind these characters. So when you’re approaching designing for Spider-Man or Wolverine, how do you strike that balance of drawing from comics or other media, but also finding that sort of distinct “Insomniac stamp” on it?
Goulden: What we always want to do is pay respect to the past, but carve our own path into the future. There’s literally decades and decades of comics and history that we can pull inspiration from, which we do. But ultimately, we want to make our own Wolverine. We want to make our own Spider-Man. We want our take on it. And when we’re doing that, we think about, “Well, what’s important for the character?” And that’s visually, too. “What are landmarks that everybody is familiar with on character designs or locations that you’d have?” And while those still say true, our take on it can become our unique twist. So I wouldn’t necessarily say there’s a lot of pressure or anything. Really, we just want to do right by the character and by the fans that they appreciate the new take on Wolverine.
I was listening to an earlier interview you did where you were talking about Spider-Man and the unexpected amount of work that goes into all of the costumes that he has with him being such an agile character. Obviously, Wolverine’s a different character with his own distinct qualities — he’s sort of getting shred to pieces in combat, with his costume breaking and the blood and gore and all that. Were there any particular design challenges or specific things to Wolverine that you had to work around and overcome?
Goulden: I wouldn’t necessarily call them challenges; they’re kind of opportunities. But the difference between Wolverine and some of the things you would gather from the interviews from Spider-Man is that Wolverine, like you said, can get torn up. He has his healing factor where he’s healing, and that’s a new element for us, completely. Being able to carve into a character and then have it regenerate was totally new technology that we had to develop. Beyond that, it’s also body hair. [laughs] We haven’t had to render such a hairy character before, and we did it very well. Running at 60 frames per second with strand-based hair all over his body is a feat.
I actually wanted to ask about the body hair! People were really taken aback by just how detailed that was. It’s kind of a funny, full-circle moment for Insomniac because I remember there’s that great running gag in Spider-Man.
Goulden: Where he’s got three chest hairs? [laughs]
Yeah! And then you zoom in, he’s actually got three chest hairs, and now you’re doing a character —
Goulden: That has a few thousand more? [laughs]
So, I’m curious: How much work goes into the tech and design of having a lifelike, realistic body hair system?
Goulden: It’s a ton of work, and it’s between our artist and our core rendering team. Much smarter people than I am. But it’s a totally new approach to it, and it took a lot of trial and error to get it right. It’s generally new, so I can’t really get into a ton of details about it.
Playing the demo a few weeks ago at Insomniac, I really liked the different visual styles there are. When you’re going into Level 3 Rage Mode, it’s this sort of black-and-red coat of paint on the world. And even when you’re skulking around, there’s that visual element of this ephemeral blue highlight on their skeletons, which I thought was a really cool approach to “Detective Modes” in games. How did you land on how you wanted these heightened visual elements to be represented?
Goulden: Every mode needs to be distinct and register with players immediately. But then there’s also inspiration that we take from the source. So for Rage, a lot of inspiration came from “Black, White, and Blood,” the comic run. And while we didn’t go literally with that, that is the foundation of why it looks that way. So when Wolverine enters Rage, all he’s thinking of is the target, “Who am I going to fight? Who am I going to take down?” And by embracing that source, what does the gameplay need to be? We can kind of marry those two together so that the world goes black and white. It doesn’t matter. All that matters is the target.
And then for the circulatory system that you’re talking about, you’ll see red trails and stuff in Madripoor. Those are all senses. “How do you visualize Wolverine’s animalistic super senses?” And it’s we have to do it visually so that people know. Obviously, just saying that you smell something isn’t really compelling or easy to understand, so that’s sort of our translations. “How would Wolverine be able to detect a person?” He’d hear their heartbeat. “How do we visualize a heartbeat?” You show it through our ethereal kind of rendering on the character, and you have their heart pumping as you get closer to them.
I believe you’re coming up on 20 years in the industry, correct?
Goulden: I think a little over 20, actually! My very first job was doing pixel art on Motorola V300. I can barely remember it. [laughs]
That’s awesome. How has the evolution of technology over this time informed your approach to art direction in games?
Goulden: The technology changes our workflow, but at the end of the day, it’s always about heart and conveying what emotional beats are and what the gameplay beats need to be, and then using art to best sell that and make it engaging for players. So, while we’ll be able to do muscle simulations, we can render all the hair and it looks beautiful, it’s really just a tool that helps those foundational skills. So the foundation is always the same, whether it’s pixel art or super high-end rendering.
Part of what I think everyone loves about Insomniac is the sheer variety of the games that you make. You can have something that’s more cartoonish, colourful, like Sunset Overdrive or Ratchet & Clank, but then you can have something more “realistic” like Spider-Man and Wolverine. Tracing the evolution between Sunset, Spider-Man, and now Wolverine, what were some of the biggest lessons that you learned from those previous games that you’ve brought into Wolverine?
Goulden: That’s a great question. I think every project ends up having different challenges that you need to address. So with Wolverine, compared to something like Sunset, which is more, I would say, playful and alive — Wolverine is more grounded and brutal and realistic. And I think the lesson that I have learned is that art serves the project the most. So whatever the project needs, art is there to complement that and present it in the best way possible for players. And as I advanced from pixel artist, character artist, lead character artist, art director — that becomes more clear because it’s less about me and my team, and it’s more about the company and the project. So how does art play this big role to make the game a success?
What’s it been like to return to Canada after working at all of those studios in the U.S.?
Goulden: It’s great. I had lived in the States for, I want to say, 12 years or so. Definitely feeling homesick every time I’d come back to Vancouver — getting a tattoo worked on, usually in Squamish, actually. So every time I’d come back, it would just be a reminder of like how much I missed Vancouver. Insomniac became a remote-first company, so that was a great opportunity for me to move back. I took it, and no regrets. I love being back in Vancouver.
I also think a lot of people will be really jazzed to learn that one of the art directors at Insomniac on Wolverine is Canadian. It’s a great story.
Goulden: It’s crazy. Getting to work on Wolverine as a Canadian, and then getting to portray the place you love in that same game? It’s probably one of the proudest things I’ll ever get to do in my career, getting to show a place I love in digital form as itself. How many opportunities do you get to do that?
Marvel’s Wolverine releases exclusively on PS5 on September 15.
For more on the game, check out our full hands-on preview and interview with creative director Marcus Smith.

articles.title: Studie zeigt: Wer KI versteht, hat mehr Angst um seinen Arbeitsplatz – nicht weniger
articles.text:
Studie zeigt: Wer KI versteht, hat mehr Angst um seinen Arbeitsplatz – nicht weniger
Viele Menschen machen sich derzeit Sorgen um die Zukunft ihrer Arbeitsplätze. Und diese Sorgen sind nicht unberechtigt. Laut einer Mercer-Befragung von Ende Mai 2026 gehen 99 Prozent der CEOs davon aus, dass sie in den nächsten zwei Jahren Mitarbeiter:innen entlassen – und deren Jobs durch KI-Tools ersetzen werden.
KI-Studie mit „beunruhigendem“ Ergebnis
Beobachter:innen waren bisher der Annahme, dass Sorgen um einen Jobverlust wegen KI vor allem eine Folge mangelnder Information seien. Eine Studie der TU Darmstadt zeigt jetzt das Gegenteil. „Ein bemerkenswertes und gleichzeitig beunruhigendes Ergebnis“, wie Projektleiter Peter Buxmann, Professor für Wirtschaftsinformatik am Fachbereich Rechts- und Wirtschaftswissenschaften der TU Darmstadt, erklärt.
Je besser Menschen verstehen, wie KI funktioniert und was mit der Technologie möglich ist, desto größer die Sorge, beruflich unter Druck zu geraten oder den eigenen Job zu verlieren. Rund 43 Prozent der Menschen mit „sehr gutem KI-Know-how“ rechnen laut Studie damit, dass KI demnächst ihre Arbeit übernehmen könnte.
Tech-Profis erkennen Sprengkraft von KI
„Wer KI am besten versteht, erkennt auch am deutlichsten ihre Sprengkraft“, kommentiert Buxmann. Die Branche sei dafür nicht entscheidend. Vielmehr geht es darum, ob die Ergebnisse der eigenen Arbeit digitalisierbar sind.
Das gilt vor allem bei der Erstellung von Texten, Analysen, Berichten, Präsentationen, Programmcodes oder anderen digitalen Arbeitsergebnissen. Laut Buxmann sind Anwält:innen, Softwareentwickler:innen oder Social-Media-Expert:innen viel „stärker von der GenAI-Revolution betroffen“ als Handwerker:innen oder Krankenpfleger:innen.
Deutschland hat KI-Weiterbildungslücke
Derweil ist KI im Alltag zwar angekommen, wird aber vorrangig von jungen, gut ausgebildeten und männlichen Nutzer:innen verwendet. Die Forscher:innen attestieren Deutschland zudem eine „KI-Weiterbildungslücke“. Demnach sollen bisher nur 15 Prozent der Befragten an einer entsprechenden Weiterbildung teilgenommen haben.
Buxmann ist der Meinung, dass generative KI zwar auch neue Tätigkeiten hervorbringe, dies jedoch vermutlich nicht in dem Maße, in dem Stellen wegfielen. „Unternehmen und Politik sind gefordert, den Sorgen nicht mit Beschwichtigung zu begegnen, sondern mit Qualifizierung und ehrlichen Antworten auf die Fragen der Arbeitswelt von morgen“, so der Wirtschaftsinformatiker.
Der aktuelle KI-Monitor der TU Darmstadt basiert auf einer in Kooperation mit dem Meinungsforschungsinstitut YouGov durchgeführten repräsentativen Befragung von mehr als 2.000 Menschen.

articles.title: OpenAI delayed its new model’s development after the Hugging Face hack
articles.text:
After an unreleased OpenAI model wreaked enough havoc to make international headlines, OpenAI delayed the development of a different unreleased model suite, Astra, in order to shore up its safety work, the company wrote Tuesday in a blog post.
OpenAI delayed its new model’s development after the Hugging Face hack
The company is doing some AI safety damage control ahead of Astra’s release.
In July, an unreleased OpenAI model broke out of its restricted environment, finagled its way into internet access, made it possible for AI agents to secretly conspire under the company’s nose using a secret message board, and hacked into the network of AI lab Hugging Face. The attack sparked weeks of discussion and controversy inside and outside the AI industry, and AI leaders treated it as a “warning shot” for the tech’s growing capabilities and the inadequacy of its safeguards.
OpenAI said as much in its blog post, writing that although Astra wasn’t involved in the Hugging Face attack, the company had chosen to delay “parts of Astra’s development and release while we strengthened and tested protections against cyber misuse and unauthorized model actions.” OpenAI also said that Astra was the first model it had ever designated as meeting its “Ccritical cybersecurity capability threshold,“ meaning that it’s able to find and exploit security vulnerabilities in “many well-protected systems” without human guidance. That means it “requires stronger safeguards during development and before release,” OpenAI wrote.
OpenAI said that to prepare for Astra’s release — which the company has not yet provided a timeline for — the company trained it to “more reliably” say no to potentially harmful cyber requests and introduced new monitoring processes. These are likely part of the new safety guardrails that the company announced in a Hugging Face post-mortem last week, where it promised to better isolate models from the internet and to introduce “24/7 escalation and rapid response” for concerning incidents. (OpenAI didn’t find out about the Hugging Face attack until weeks after it occurred.)
Astra is significantly riskier than OpenAI’s current leading model, GPT-5.6 Sol, the company says, because it represents a big step forward in cybersecurity capabilities — specifically, it uses fewer tokens to do more work, and it’s better at finding security gaps and developing ways to exploit them. But the company also wrote that Astra was its “most aligned model to date” according to internal evaluations.
OpenAI also said it had developed a test inspired by the Hugging Face attack, in which it tried to entreat agents to compromise security infrastructure instead of solving a task. It said GPT-5.6 Sol took the bait in more than half of the tests, but Astra “made no such attempts.”

articles.title: Gal Gadot (Wonder Woman) ataca a James Gunn y su nuevo 'Universo DC': "No han sido elegantes"
articles.text:
El nuevo Universo DC de James Gunn y Peter Safran sigue sin presentar a su próxima Wonder Woman. Pero, mientras los fans esperan pacientemente, la anterior actriz de la superheroína, Gal Gadot, ha roto por fin su silencio sobre la renovada franquicia. Y sus palabras no han sido especialmente amables hacia los directivos de la compañía. De hecho, ha criticado con dureza su gestión.
Cuando James Gunn y Peter Safran se hicieron cargo del Universo DC, se anunció de manera no oficial Wonder Woman 3, de nuevo con Gal Gadot como protagonista y la directora Patty Jenkins a los mandos. Sin embargo, el proyecto se canceló rápidamente. Y ahora, la actriz ha hablado sobre lo sucedido.
"A mí me dijeron justo lo contrario. Me dijeron algo así como: “Vamos a desarrollar [Wonder Woman 3] contigo”. Pero vi cómo se trató a todos los demás, ¿verdad? La situación de Henry Cavill no se gestionó con elegancia, por decirlo suavemente. Lo mismo ocurrió con Patty. No se gestionó con elegancia", critica Gal Gadot en una entrevista concedida al podcast Happy, Sad, Confused.
"Todos somos adultos, está todo bien. Y ni siquiera se trata de ellos. Están ahí, y están ahí para defender aquello en lo que creen, así que está todo bien. Estoy muy agradecida por haber tenido la oportunidad de llevar estas botas, de que el personaje haya sido tan aclamado y haya sido el vehículo en ese momento concreto", se consuela en cualquier caso.
La nueva actriz de Wonder Woman
A su vez, Gal Gadot también ha querido comentar acerca de la nueva actriz de Wonder Woman en el Universo DC. Aún no se sabe quién será, pero ella ha querido dedicarle unas palabras. "Solo puedo desear que quienquiera que sea se embarque en este viaje lo haga con el corazón puro. Porque por mucho que parezca que estamos hablando de películas y superhéroes y bla, bla, bla, este personaje significa realmente mucho para muchos de nosotros", asegura.
"Que lo use de verdad con respeto y aporte todo el amor y la luz que pueda a este mundo. Disfruta del viaje. Nunca fue mía. Yo siempre fui solo un vehículo. Esto es Hollywood", añade, confiada de que la próxima actriz de Wonder Woman pueda estar a la altura. Porque lo cierto es que, aunque le pidieran regresar, Gal Gadot ya no se ve de nuevo en el personaje.
"Mira, todo depende del guion y, normalmente, del director. Creo que si tuviera que hacer, por ejemplo, otra película de Wonder Woman, no estoy segura de que pudiera en esta etapa de mi vida, con cuatro hijos, con sus diferentes colegios y todo eso, tener que estar pendiente de todos ellos durante un periodo de tiempo tan largo. A estas alturas, ya no encaja con mi vida", sentencia.

articles.title: AIR raises $50M to help companies vet the skills and add-ons AI agents use | TechCrunch
articles.text:
As companies start giving AI agents access to an increasing portion of their systems, a nascent software supply chain seems to be forming around the new tooling AI agents are using: skills, plug-ins, MCP servers, and add-ons that let them interact with the internet.
AI security startup AIR believes companies will need a way to monitor that supply chain, and it’s now coming out of stealth with $50 million raised across two seed rounds to build that product.
Founded by Yair Saban (CEO) and Niv Hoffman (CTO), veterans of Israel’s Unit 8200 intelligence corps, where they worked on offensive cybersecurity, AIR offers a platform that can discover agents running inside companies, continuously vet any skills, tools, and components those agents use, and block them from interacting with software or external sources that don’t pass security criteria. It also offers a marketplace of vetted add-ons and skills for AI agents.
The funding rounds closed within weeks of each other, Saban told TechCrunch, with the first round raising $10 million, and the second $40 million. Sequoia led the first round, while Greenoaks led the second, Saban said. Swish, Netz, and Zach Frankel (president of Cognition), Yinon Costica (co-founder of Wiz), Ofir Ehrlich (co-founder of Eon), Anne Neuberger, Omer Adam, Varun Anand (co-founder of Clay), and other angel investors also participated.
AIR’s pitch goes thusly: The way AI agents are used wholesale at companies is beginning to resemble operating systems, but the tools they use, or the software they can install, aren’t yet being given the kind of oversight we give to drivers or applications.
“In the early 2000s, whenever you installed a driver, the driver didn’t need to be signed. Today, every time you install a driver, you see a signature saying who signed it, because the driver is actually loading code into the kernel,” Saban said. “You don’t have that with skills or plug-ins or MCPs, and it’s a shame, because it’s the same mechanism, it’s the same lesson, but we haven’t learned it.”
The big risk, he argues, is that as AI agents start working more autonomously across databases and enterprise systems, and connecting to the internet, attackers can poison the content an AI agent consumes instead of attacking it directly.
The startup says it can solve that with a visibility product that finds agents active across a company’s environment, as well as identifies employees who use AI tools unapproved by IT departments or those who use personal accounts. Then, it uses an enforcement layer that hooks into agents to intercept and analyze actions, like loading a skill or fetching content from the internet. Lastly, AIR also checks the tools, add-ons, or software an agent wants to use against a whitelist the startup maintains.
Saban says the startup maintains this whitelist by evaluating skills and add-ons openly available on the internet for changes and malicious behavior, as a previously approved skill could become risky if a package it downloads changes, or its developer’s account is compromised. He added that AIR’s platform currently filters out about 27% of the add-ons and skills it finds online.
AIR claims it has more than 20 customers, and Saban said roughly a quarter of these are large enterprises. He said the company has so far seen the strongest demand in heavily regulated industries, particularly financial services and pharmaceutical companies.
However, AIR is hardly alone in this space. Noma Security offers discovery, access controls, and runtime monitoring for agents, MCP servers, and skills, while Zenity sells security and governance tools that work similarly. Astrix Security‘s identity platform also lets companies discover and control agents and MCP servers, and Operant AI offers agent protections as well as an MCP gateway.
There is significant venture money chasing the category, too. Zenity raised a $125 million Series C in August, while Noma raised a $100 million Series B last year.
Saban thinks AIR’s moat lies in its ability to continuously vet the skills and add-ons ecosystem growing around AI agents. “Continuously vetting skills and plug-in websites, this is a hard mission to do. Gaining visibility over the endpoint, that is easy. Everybody’s going to do it. It’s hard to create a moat around that,” he said.
And while the CEO acknowledged that AI labs and providers will eventually build in security checks and policies to filter out malicious skill and tool usage, he thinks companies will still want to buy an independent product that works across vendors.
“This is not a scanning problem, it is a continuous re-verification problem,” Bogomil Balkansky, partner at Sequoia, told TechCrunch in an emailed statement. “Inspecting every skill, plugin, MCP server and sub-agent an enterprise’s agents touch, re-inspecting each one every time it changes, in real time and across an entire company’s agent fleet, is an infrastructure problem long before it is a security problem. Air has spent the last year building that pipeline. You do not catch up to it by writing a better scanner.”
AIR currently has around 40 employees. Saban said the new capital will primarily go toward hiring researchers and expanding the company’s go-to-market efforts in the U.S. and Europe.

articles.title: Sonos introduces new Beam Ultra soundbar and Ace Ultra headphones - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Sonos has expanded the home theatre and personal listening ranges with two new products – the Sonos Beam Ultra and the Sonos Ace Ultra.
Sonos has also upgraded its audio operating system to Sonos 27.
The Beam Ultra soundbar has retained its compact design but has unlocked 7.1.2 Dolby Atmos while the Sonos Ace Ultra headphones feature an all-new driver and improved ANC (active noise cancellation).
“Beam Ultra and Sonos Ace Ultra are physical manifestations of what we mean when we say ‘sounds like Sonos’ – they combine next-gen innovation, acoustic design, and audio
engineering into something only decades of learning in real homes can create,” says Tom Conrad, CEO of Sonos.
“But the real magic happens when they take advantage of the system around them to fit your mood, whether that’s the awe of movie night, or the joy of carrying its soundtrack into your headphones the next morning.”
SONOS BEAM ULTRA – $1,099
The new Sonos midsize soundbar has nine custom built drivers including two dedicated upfiring drivers to provide 7.1.2 Dolby Atmos and improved bass.
The centre channel has been redesigned to offer clearer, crisper dialogue which has four levels of AI enhancement.
Beam Ultra can be the centre of a home theatre set up that can grow and adapt to your needs by adding a Sub or rear and surround speakers.
SONOS ACE ULTRA – $699
The latest Sonos premium over-ear headphones have been engineered with a new 40mm driver and improved Adaptive ANC that is powered by 10 microphones.
It is the first pair of headphones built on Headphone Engine 2 – a new hardware platform that allows them to link directly to a Sonos system.
With one press you can direct whatever is playing on your Sonos system and direct them to your Sonos headphones without the need to reach for your phone or an app.
The Sonos Beam Ultra ($1,099) and Sonos Ace Ultra ($699) are available to pre-order now and will go on sale on September 29, 2026.

articles.title: When agents build, deploy, and maintain, persistence becomes the hard problem
articles.text:
When agents build, deploy, and maintain, persistence becomes the hard problem
Every application has always needed a place to keep its state. That is not new. What is new is who creates that place, how many get created, and how long they have to survive after everyone has stopped looking.
“Separating durable state from ephemeral compute is the new requirement, and the idle cost trap is only half of it.”
Consider the agents built by Kimi, the AI platform from Moonshot AI. A non-technical user describes an application in plain language. An agent builds the frontend, backend, and database, then deploys them in minutes. The user never thinks about infrastructure. They asked for a tool and received a running one.
Then the agent does something the previous generation of coding assistants never did. It does not hand over code and walk away. It keeps the application running and comes back to maintain it. That last word is where the old assumptions break. Build once and hand off, and state is almost an afterthought.
Build, deploy, and maintain across tens of millions of applications, most idle most of the time, and persistence stops being a database feature and becomes the central economic problem of the whole system.
I have written before about what happens to a database when its user is an agent rather than a human. Kimi is the clearest production example I have seen, and it surfaces a requirement that the industry has not really been asked to meet: keep state alive cheaply in two very different places at once. The problem is not performance. It is the economics of persistence.
The number that changes the question
When you serve thousands of tenants, the questions are familiar. How fast are queries? How do we fail over? How do we back up? The industry has good answers for all of them. When you serve tens of millions, most created by agents and most idle most of the time, a different question moves to the front, and it is the one nobody planned for: what does it cost to keep something alive that nobody is using right now?
Ask it once, and you are talking about idle databases. Ask it again, one layer up, and you are talking about the agent’s own half-finished work sitting between maintenance sessions. Same question, two surfaces. At a thousand you absorb it. At ten thousand it stings. At tens of millions it is fatal.
“In a human-driven product, what you provision and what people use track each other. In an agent-driven product, they diverge wildly.”
This is the shift agents force. In a human-driven product, what you provision and what people use track each other. In an agent-driven product, they diverge wildly, because agents create far faster and more casually than humans ever did, and most of what they create goes idle immediately.
One principle, two places
There is a single move underneath everything that follows: separate durable state from ephemeral compute. State is the part you must never lose, so it belongs on a shared, cheap, effectively infinite foundation.
I have argued before that object storage is becoming the new network layer of the data stack, and this is what that looks like, built for agents: durable data at rest costs almost nothing. Compute is the part you should be able to throw away, summoned when work arrives and released when it stops.
Couple the two and you pay to keep compute running for state that is doing nothing. Decouple them, and your cost stops tracking how much you have created and starts tracking how much work is happening.
Every hard number in the Kimi deployment comes from getting this separation right in the two places an agent-scale product needs it: the databases the agent provisions for its users and the workspace the agent lives in.
The first place: the idle tenant
The instinct most teams start with is the one that has worked for a decade: give each tenant its own database instance. It is clean and easy to reason about. Kimi’s earlier shape was close to this, with single-instance PostgreSQL behind the product. It works beautifully until the tenant count climbs into the tens of thousands, and then the economics invert. The reason is structural.
A per-tenant instance couples the logical experience of an isolated database to the physical reality of dedicated, always-on compute. The tenant needs the first. The business cannot afford the second at scale. Cost grows with tenants created, not tenants active, and in an agent-driven product those two numbers are worlds apart.
“The agent experiences a dedicated, isolated database, while a virtual layer beneath provides each one its own namespace. The agent does not need a dedicated instance. It needs the experience of one.”
I have started calling this the idle cost trap, because teams walk into it without seeing it, and by the time they feel it, the architecture that created it is load-bearing. The way out is the principle. The agent experiences a dedicated, isolated database, while a virtual layer beneath provides each one its own namespace and isolation guarantees over a shared substrate, with object storage holding durable data and a routing layer sending requests where they belong. The agent does not need a dedicated instance. It needs the experience of one.
There is a catch worth being honest about. If compute is summoned on demand, then when a request arrives for an idle tenant something has to spin up, and if that is slow, you have traded a cost problem for a latency problem.
Kimi provisions a database in about a second, from a warm pool of pre-initialized resources kept ready and replenished behind each claim, so database setup drops out of the delivery pipeline entirely. That number is not a benchmark to brag about. It is the evidence that ephemeral compute over shared, persistent storage can stand in for the always-on model, because it appears fast enough to feel always-on.
The second place: the agent’s own workspace
The maintenance half of the lifecycle drags the same problem into a place most teams never look: the agent’s own working environment. An agent that builds once can treat its workspace as disposable: spin up a sandbox, write code, ship, discard. An agent that maintains cannot work that way.
It has to return days or weeks later and pick up where it left off: source code, Git history, checkpoints, the record of what it was in the middle of doing. If that context is lost, the agent does not resume work. It is reconstructing it.
And execution environments are ephemeral on purpose, because keeping millions alive between sessions is the idle cost trap in a different costume. So the environment gets torn down. If the work goes with it, every maintenance session begins by rebuilding state the agent already had: wasted compute, wasted tokens, and a user watching an agent relearn its own project.
The fix is the same separation, one layer up. Kimi uses a persistent filesystem that keeps development state alive independently of the compute that produced it. Source code, Git history, checkpoints, and task progress persist after the environment is destroyed, so the agent resumes rather than starting over. Compute is ephemeral and cheap to discard. State is durable and cheap to keep. Same trade as the idle tenant, seen from the builder’s side.
The database choice becomes a quality input
There is a further effect that surprised me, because it shows up in the quality of what the agent builds. Every infrastructure decision is a chance to get something wrong. If each task forces the agent to reason from scratch about which database to use and how to configure it, it is improvising on every run, and improvisation is where errors enter.
When the stack is unified, it applies known-good patterns instead. Kimi saw code generation success rates improve from standardizing on a unified data layer, and that is the mechanism: fewer places for the output to go wrong.
“The choice of database is no longer just an infrastructure decision. It is a quality input to the agent’s work.”
This is a version of an argument I keep returning to. Agents need guardrails, and the most effective ones are built into the infrastructure rather than bolted on as instructions. A database that behaves consistently every time is a guardrail. The choice of database is no longer just an infrastructure decision. It is a quality input to the agent’s work.
Four properties that have never been requried together
Step back from Kimi and the shape of the requirement is clear. An agent-scale product needs four things from its data layer at once:
- Tenant isolation: every agent-created database must be logically separate, so millions of tenants never bleed into one another.
- Instant provisioning: a new tenant has to exist in about a second, because an agent will not wait and neither will the user behind it.
- Cost elasticity: an idle tenant, and an idle workspace, has to cost almost nothing, because most things are idle most of the time.
- Persistent state independent of compute: the tenant’s data and the agent’s development state alike must survive the ephemeral environments that produced them.
Each has been solved before in isolation. Databases have offered isolation for decades. Serverless systems provision quickly. Object storage is cheap at rest. What is new is the demand for all four at once, at a scale where any one failing breaks the product. That is the real infrastructure competition of the agent era, and it is not the one the industry is used to having. It is not about who has the fastest single query. It is about who can hold all four together at tens of millions of tenants without one collapsing the others.
The pattern is bigger than one product
I do not think Kimi is a special case. It is an early, unusually clear instance of a pattern that will repeat across every product where agents build for non-technical users at scale. The shape is always the same. One agent, one workspace, one database, repeated millions of times. Each instance feels independent.
The infrastructure underneath is shared, and it works only because a virtual layer separates the logical experience of isolation from the physical cost of compute, and because durable state is allowed to outlive the compute that produced it.
Kimi is the version where the agent hands a finished application to an end user and then stays on to maintain it, which is harder in two ways at once. The tenant does not go away when the run ends; it persists, idle, waiting, multiplied by tens of millions. And the agent does not go away either, so its own working state has to survive every gap between sessions. Persistence is no longer a property of one component. It is the property the whole system is organized around.
“The database conversation in the agent era is no longer really about speed. Get it wrong, and no amount of model quality will save the margins.”
Teams building in this direction will hit the idle cost trap on both surfaces, whether they plan for it or not. The only choice is whether they see it coming. Design for all four from the start and you scale past the point where the per-tenant-instance model collapses. Do not, and you hit that ceiling at tens of thousands of tenants, exactly where Kimi’s earlier architecture did, and sooner than you expect, because agents fill a tenant table faster than any human-driven product ever has.
The database conversation in the agent era is no longer really about speed. It is about whether the economics of persistence can survive the scale that agents create in both the database and the workspace. Get that right early, and the rest of the product has room to grow. Get it wrong, and no amount of model quality will save the margins.
If you are building a product where agents provision infrastructure for end users and then stay on to maintain it, four things make that economically viable: isolation, instant provisioning, near-zero idle cost, and durable state on a shared substrate. That is what we have built into TiDB’s serverless and agent workloads. It is the pattern these teams keep arriving at from different directions.

articles.title: Product Configuration Guide for Electronics Manufacturers - EE Times
articles.text:
Product configuration makes it possible for electronics manufacturers to offer different product variants without engineering every order from scratch. By defining options and compatibility rules in advance, manufacturers can give customers more choice while keeping BOMs, assembly processes, purchasing, testing, and production manageable.
What is product configuration?
Product configuration is the process of adapting a product to a customer’s requirements using predefined options and rules.
In electronics manufacturing, this could mean allowing customers to choose between different power supplies, communication modules, I/O configurations, displays, enclosures, connectors, firmware packages, or accessories while keeping the underlying product architecture standardized.
Configuration rules ensure that incompatible combinations cannot be selected and that each resulting product can actually be manufactured. When product configuration is connected with manufacturing software, the selected configuration can also determine the appropriate BOM, routing, material requirements, production costs, and lead time.
Product configuration is closely associated with mass customization, where manufacturers offer customers a degree of personalization without taking on the cost and complexity of designing every order from scratch.
Product configuration example
Consider a manufacturer producing industrial electronic controllers.
Customers might start with the same base product but choose between:
- Different input voltages
- Standard or extended I/O
- Ethernet, Wi-Fi, CAN bus, or other communication options
- Different displays or user interfaces
- Alternative enclosure types
- Region-specific power supplies or connectors
- Optional sensors, modules, or accessories
- Different firmware packages
Creating a separate BOM manually for every possible combination would quickly become difficult to manage.
With a configurable or matrix BOM, the manufacturer can define the available options and the components associated with each one. When a configuration is selected, the manufacturing system generates the appropriate BOM for that specific unit or order.
For example, choosing an Ethernet communications module could add the corresponding PCB module and connector to the BOM, while selecting an industrial enclosure could add different mounting hardware and assembly operations.
The manufacturer gets the flexibility of multiple product variants without maintaining hundreds of independent BOMs.
Chris Landen, COO at UK-based computer hardware manufacturer Exacta Technologies, says, “Our product set is large and complex. MRPeasy allows us to manage multi-level and configurable BOMs while controlling revisions and engineering changes properly.”
Sales configuration vs product configuration
Product configuration and sales configuration are closely related, but they serve different purposes.
Product configuration defines what can be manufactured. It covers the available features, modules, components, accessories, and the technical rules governing how they can be combined.
Sales configuration determines which of those options can be offered and quoted to a customer. This is commonly handled through configure, price, quote (CPQ) software.
For example, an electronics manufacturer may have engineering rules specifying which power supply works with a particular board and enclosure. A salesperson using CPQ does not need to know those dependencies manually. The configuration system can restrict the available choices and calculate the resulting price.
Connecting product and sales configuration helps prevent sales teams from quoting product combinations that engineering or production cannot build.
Benefits of product configuration for electronics manufacturers
More efficient engineering and production
Electronics manufacturers often sell families of products built around common PCBs, modules, housings, power supplies, and other components.
Without a structured configuration system, every variation can create additional work. Engineering may need to check specifications, production may need clarification about which revision or component goes into the build, and purchasing may have to interpret requirements manually.
Product configuration standardizes these decisions.
Engineering defines valid combinations in advance. Production receives the correct BOM and assembly requirements. Purchasing can see the specific components required for the order.
This reduces the amount of manual coordination needed each time a customer requests a different variation of an existing product.
Sales can also benefit. When CPQ and manufacturing software are connected, salespeople can configure a valid product and use current manufacturing data to estimate its cost and lead time. This reduces back-and-forth with engineering before a quote can be sent.
Better quality control
Quality control becomes more difficult when every electronic product is effectively a one-off.
Different boards, components, firmware versions, connectors, and testing requirements can make it harder to standardize inspection and testing procedures.
Product configuration creates repeatable product variants. Manufacturers can define the correct assembly and testing requirements for each configuration and reuse them whenever that variant is produced.
For example, a specific configuration might require a particular functional test, firmware version, calibration procedure, or final inspection step.
Repeatedly producing the same validated configurations also makes recurring quality problems easier to identify and correct.
Less rework and scrap
Mistakes in electronics manufacturing can be expensive.
An incorrect component, incompatible module, wrong connector, or unsuitable power supply may require PCB rework or even make an assembly unusable.
Configuration rules can prevent many of these errors before the manufacturing order reaches production.
Teams work from predefined configurations, configurable BOMs, and validated production processes rather than interpreting customer requirements from scratch for each order.
The more often a configuration is produced, the easier it also becomes to identify problems in assembly, testing, or component selection and correct them at the source.
Lower inventory requirements
Electronics manufacturers with many product variants can easily end up carrying too many finished SKUs.
One controller might be available with four communication options, three enclosure types, two displays, and several accessory packages. Stocking every possible finished configuration would require a large amount of inventory, even if some combinations rarely sell.
Product configuration makes an assemble-to-order (ATO) approach more practical.
Instead of stocking every finished variant, the manufacturer can hold common PCBs, modules, enclosures, components, and subassemblies. The final configuration is assembled once the customer places an order.
This reduces finished-goods inventory while still allowing the company to offer a broad range of product variants.
Better management of components
Component management is a particular challenge in electronics manufacturing. Availability, lead times, and prices can change quickly, and a single component shortage can affect several products.
A structured configuration system makes it easier to understand which components are required by each product variant.
When configuration is connected with inventory and purchasing data, manufacturers can see whether the components required for an order are available before committing production resources.
Where approved alternative components exist, manufacturers can also manage substitutions more systematically rather than making ad hoc changes on the shop floor.
Faster and more reliable quoting
Electronics quotes can become complicated when product choices affect both material and production costs.
Adding another communications board, changing the enclosure, or selecting a different power supply can change:
- Component costs
- Assembly time
- Testing requirements
- Outside processing
- Purchasing requirements
- Lead time
With structured product configuration, these requirements can be associated with the chosen options.
A connected CPQ or manufacturing ERP system, such as MRPeasy, can then use the resulting BOM and routing to calculate estimated costs and lead times, giving sales teams a much stronger basis for quoting configurable products.
Better customer experience
Customers get more choice without needing to order a completely custom product.
They can select the communications, interfaces, enclosure, accessories, or other features that fit their application while staying within the combinations the manufacturer has already designed and validated.
Configuration can also make quoting faster because sales teams do not need to send every variation through engineering before responding.
For manufacturers selling configurable electronics online, product configurators can allow customers to select compatible options directly through an e-commerce site.
Challenges of product configuration
Defining configuration rules
The hardest part of setting up product configuration is often defining the rules themselves.
Electronics products can have dependencies involving:
- PCB revisions
- Electronic components
- Power requirements
- Connectors
- Communication protocols
- Enclosures
- Displays
- Firmware
- Accessories
- Assembly processes
- Testing procedures
Manufacturers need to determine which combinations are technically valid and turn that engineering knowledge into structured configuration rules.
Those rules also need to account for commercial considerations. A configuration may be technically possible but too expensive, difficult to source, or inefficient to manufacture as a standard option.
Managing component substitutions
Electronics manufacturers frequently need to replace components because of shortages, obsolescence, price changes, or supplier changes.
This creates an extra layer of configuration complexity.
An alternative component may fit physically but require a different PCB revision, a firmware change, a different testing procedure, or a certification review. Manufacturers therefore need clear processes for defining which substitutions are approved and where they can be used.
Configuration rules and BOM version control can help keep these changes under control.
Too many product options
Offering more options does not always create more value.
A manufacturer might technically be able to offer dozens of combinations of boards, displays, enclosures, interfaces, and accessories. But every additional option creates more product data, configuration rules, purchasing requirements, documentation, testing, and support work.
Too many choices can also make the buying process difficult for customers.
The goal should be to offer configurations that address real customer requirements while keeping the number of combinations manageable.
Product and engineering data requirements
Product configuration depends on accurate product data.
In electronics manufacturing, that data can include BOMs, component specifications, revisions, approved alternatives, routing times, assembly instructions, firmware versions, test procedures, costs, and configuration dependencies.
The difficulty is that this information changes.
A component can become obsolete. A PCB can move to a new revision. A supplier can change its price. A new firmware release may support different hardware. An alternative component may be approved.
If configuration rules are not updated along with these changes, manufacturers can end up producing or quoting products based on outdated information.
Disconnected systems
Electronics manufacturers may keep product information across several systems.
Engineering data may live in ECAD or PLM software. Customer information may sit in a CRM. Manufacturing BOMs and inventory may be managed in an ERP system. Shop floor data may be handled elsewhere.
When these systems are disconnected, engineering, sales, purchasing, and production can end up working from different versions of the same product information.
Product configuration systems for electronics manufacturers
Configurable BOMs as the foundation of product configuration
For electronics manufacturers, a configurable BOM, sometimes called a matrix BOM, provides the manufacturing foundation for product configuration.
Instead of creating a completely separate BOM for every possible product variant, the configurable BOM contains the components and options required across the product family.
For example, a configurable BOM for an industrial controller might contain:
- Base PCB assembly
- Alternative processor boards
- Communication modules
- I/O modules
- Display options
- Power supplies
- Connectors
- Enclosures
- Mounting hardware
- Accessories
Rules determine which components are included when a specific configuration is selected.
If the customer chooses cellular connectivity, the generated BOM might include the cellular module and antenna. If they choose Ethernet instead, those components are replaced by the Ethernet-specific parts.
The manufacturing system can then create the BOM required for the selected configuration without the manufacturer maintaining every possible combination as a separate product structure.
Manufacturing ERP software for product configuration
A configurable BOM becomes much more useful when it is connected to the rest of the manufacturing operation.
Manufacturing ERP software such as MRPeasy connects BOM data with inventory, purchasing, production planning, costing, and sales.
When a configurable product is ordered, the ERP system can generate the appropriate BOM and use it to determine which materials are required.
It can then compare those requirements with inventory levels and identify shortages. Required components can be purchased, while available materials can be allocated to production.
The resulting manufacturing order gives production a clear definition of what needs to be built.
This connection is particularly valuable for electronics manufacturers because a relatively small configuration change can affect components, costs, purchasing requirements, assembly operations, and testing.
Instead of updating those areas manually, configuration data can flow through the manufacturing system from the BOM.
Configure, price, quote (CPQ)
Configure, price, quote (CPQ) software gives sales teams a structured way to select product options, calculate prices, and prepare customer quotes.
For an electronics manufacturer, a CPQ interface might allow a salesperson to select the required power input, I/O, communications, enclosure, and accessories.
Configuration rules prevent incompatible choices from being quoted.
When CPQ is integrated with manufacturing ERP software, manufacturing data can also feed into the quote. Depending on the systems involved, this can include component costs, material availability, production requirements, and estimated lead times.
Once the customer approves the quote, the configured product data can be transferred into the manufacturing process instead of being entered again manually.
This reduces duplicate data entry and the risk of differences between what sales quoted and what production was instructed to build.
E-commerce integrations
Product configurators can also be used on e-commerce websites.
An electronics manufacturer selling standardized configurable products could allow customers to choose options such as enclosure type, communication interface, cable length, accessories, or power supply directly on the website.
Rules can hide or block incompatible combinations and adjust pricing according to the selected options.
Some manufacturing ERP systems integrate with e-commerce platforms such as Shopify and WooCommerce. Orders can then be transferred from the online store into the manufacturing system without manually re-entering the customer and product information.
For relatively standardized electronic products, this can create a direct path from customer configuration to manufacturing while still keeping production based on controlled BOMs and predefined product options.

articles.title: Tim Cook passe le relais après 15 ans à la tête d’Apple et livre son dernier message
articles.text:
Quinze ans après avoir pris les commandes d’Apple, Tim Cook s’apprête à tourner une page majeure de son histoire au sein du groupe. À la veille de passer le relais à John Ternus, le futur président exécutif a adressé un dernier message à ses équipes et à la communauté Apple.
Le 1ᵉʳ septembre 2026 marque la fin d'une ère pour la marque à la pomme. John Ternus, jusqu'ici responsable de l'ingénierie hardware, prend la direction générale d'Apple. La veille de cette passation de pouvoir, Cook a publié une note interne destinée aux salariés, rendue publique par 9to5Mac, ainsi qu'un message sur les réseaux sociaux adressé aux clients. Deux prises de parole placées sous le signe de la gratitude et de la continuité.
Tim Cook rend hommage à ses équipes dans un dernier mémo
Dans son dernier message adressé aux salariés, Tim Cook ne s’attarde pas sur les résultats obtenus par Apple durant ses quinze années à la tête du groupe. Il préfère plutôt mettre en avant ceux qui les ont rendus possibles. « Quelle que soit la façon dont on juge mon succès, je sais qu’il vous revient entièrement. Vous avez tiré le meilleur de moi », écrit-il, avant de rendre hommage à une équipe qu’il décrit comme exceptionnelle.
Pour Tim Cook, qui avait pris la suite de Steve Jobs en 2011, ce qui fait la force d’Apple ne se résume d’ailleurs pas à ses produits ou à ses performances financières. « Cet endroit est la preuve que la culture prime sur tout le reste », affirme-t-il. Cook insiste sur cette volonté commune de concevoir des produits qui comptent, mais également sur la responsabilité de contribuer à rendre le monde meilleur. Une vision qu’il attribue autant à l’entreprise qu’aux personnes qui la composent.
Quitter un poste qu’il a profondément aimé ne sera toutefois pas simple, même s’il se dit pleinement serein face à sa décision. Il dit par ailleurs avoir toute confiance en John Ternus, à qui il s’apprête à confier les commandes d’Apple : « Je ne pourrais pas être plus enthousiaste à l’idée de confier les rênes à quelqu’un d’aussi brillant et capable que John ».
Après le fauteuil de PDG, Tim Cook ouvre un nouveau chapitre de son histoire chez Apple
Si Tim Cook quitte bien la direction générale, il ne quitte pas pour autant l’entreprise qu’il a dirigée pendant quinze ans. Depuis ce 1ᵉʳ septembre, il est donc président exécutif d’Apple et continue d’exercer ses fonctions au sein du groupe. Il l’avait d’ailleurs rappelé sans ambiguïté à ses salariés : « Je ne quitte pas Apple », tout en précisant qu’il se retirait d’un rôle qu’il a profondément aimé.
Le changement de titre ne l’empêchera pas non plus de rester proche de l’entreprise. Dans son message, Cook explique qu’il a hâte de retrouver ses équipes dans son nouveau rôle, à Apple Park comme lors de ses déplacements à travers le monde.
Il s’est également adressé directement à la communauté Apple sur les réseaux sociaux, avec un message plus court et personnel. « Mon titre change demain, mais l’amour que j’ai pour la communauté Apple ne changera jamais », a-t-il écrit, avant de remercier les utilisateurs pour leur inspiration et d’évoquer avec un enthousiasme non dissimulé « le prochain chapitre ».
Une page se tourne donc chez Apple, mais Tim Cook ne disparaît pas totalement du décor. Après quinze longues années à incarner le groupe, son dernier message comme PDG ressemble moins à un adieu qu’à un passage de témoin.

articles.title: Kepler Aerospace bags $8M to deploy swarming satellites
articles.text:
Kepler Aerospace bags $8M to deploy swarming satellites
Bengaluru-based Kepler Aerospace will use the seed funding to deploy six swarming ISR satellites and expand its mission operations and avionics businesses.
Kepler Aerospace, a space infrastructure and mission operations company, has raised $8 million in a seed round led by Blue Ashva Capital and co-led by Finvolve India Accelerator and other investors.
The Bengaluru-based firm plans to use the capital primarily to deploy the first six satellites in its autonomous swarming intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance programme under India’s Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) initiative. It has secured two iDEX prime contracts and received about $4 million in grants under the programme.
The fresh funding will also support the expansion of its Mission Operations as a Service and Avionics as a Service businesses, as well as engineering capacity. Over the next 12 to 24 months, the company plans to move into a new facility and add 40 employees.
Kepler’s proposition goes beyond building satellites. It is developing an integrated stack covering satellite systems, avionics, ground infrastructure, mission operations and intelligence delivery.
According to the company, its mission operations platform already serves nearly all Indian space companies, and it operates several ISRO satellites. Its network of more than 70 ground stations provides communications, tracking, telemetry and command functions.
A swarming constellation allows multiple satellites to coordinate their activities, potentially reducing reliance on instructions from a ground station and shortening the time between collecting information and acting on it.
Founder and chief executive officer Navneet Singh said national security will increasingly depend on the ability to “see, understand and respond faster”, adding that achieving this requires satellites, avionics, ground systems and mission operations to function as one system.
Blue Ashva founder Satya Bansal noted that the company’s autonomous architecture could allow satellites to “task each other and act in orbit” without waiting for a ground station.
The fundraise comes as India’s private space industry broadens well beyond launch vehicles. Government data put cumulative private investment in the sector at $618.5 million by March 2026, while the number of registered spacetech startups had reached about 440 by August. Recent funding rounds includes Rs 100 crore by InspeCity, $60 million by unicorn Skyroot, and $20 million by Bellatrix.
Policy has also helped reshape the market, with India opening the sector to private participation in 2020, creating IN-SPACe as the authorising and supervisory body, and subsequently liberalising foreign investment rules for space activities.
The government has also established a Rs 1,000 crore space venture capital fund, alongside seed funding and technology-support programmes. The result is a shift towards a more active ecosystem that is heading towards commercialisation.

articles.title: Hackers push malicious Virtualizor update in BGP hijacking attack
articles.text:
Hackers delivered malicious updates to the Virtualizor VPS management software after hijacking BGP routing for its update infrastructure and redirecting update requests to malicious servers.
Virtualizor is a legacy web control panel from Softaculous that hosting providers use to create, sell, and manage virtual private servers (VPS).
An urgent notice from the vendor warns that between 20:57 UTC on August 28 and 06:10 UTC on August 30, an attacker rerouted a block of Hetzner-hosted IP addresses in a BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) hijacking attack.
This enabled the threat actor to divert traffic from Softaculous software update systems and the client/billing portal.
BGP hijacking occurs when a network operator falsely announces a route to IP addresses belonging to another organization. Other organizations may accept the fraudulent route as the preferred one.
An attacker receiving traffic this way can modify or redirect it to malicious destinations.
Softaculous says that the BGP hijacking allowed the hackers to deliver a malicious Virtualizor update to a small number of installations.
“We have confirmed that a malicious Virtualizor update package was delivered to a small number of installations that checked for updates while their traffic was being diverted,” the vendor says.
“This affected a handful of servers rather than the general Virtualizor user base.”
Because the requests were redirected to the attacker, the software vendor does not have logs. Softaculous recommends that Virtualizor operators check for the service:
/etc/systemd/system/java-jre-update.service
If found, admins should rotate and restrict API credentials, and audit systems for unauthorized SSH keys, accounts, scheduled tasks, and outbound connections.
Also, users who accessed the Softaculous client area or entered payment information during the incident window should reset their passwords, review account activity, and monitor card statements.
Softaculous's investigation into the incident is still underway, but there are no indications that any of its other products were impacted.
Softaculous says routing has now been restored, the fraudulent certificate was reported for revocation, and a new version of Virtualizor, number 3.2.9.9, was released on September 1 with a “Security Analyzer” tool in the admin panel.
The company also plans to implement cryptographic signing for all software packages going forward and migrate to better infrastructure.

articles.title: Vague d'arnaques en France : la Caisse des Dépôts alerte sur une « tentative de fraude » avec « faux conseillers »
articles.text:
La Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations (CDC) tire la sonnette d’alarme. Dans un avertissement publié sur son site web, l’institution financière publique indique qu’une vague d’arnaques « au nom de la Caisse des Dépôts » est en cours en France. Le communiqué, publié le lundi 31 août 2026, parle d’une série de tentatives de fraude.
À lire aussi : Fuites de données – Lecornu donne « quinze jours » à ses ministres pour riposter
De faux conseillers s’en prennent aux Français
Pour tenter de piéger les Français, les cybercriminels se font passer pour de « faux conseillers Caisse des Dépôts ». Comme toujours, les truands usurpent l’identité d’une entité de confiance pour arriver à leurs fins. L’escroquerie vise des particuliers, qui ne font pas partie des clients de la Caisse des Dépôts.
La cyberattaque s’appuie sur plusieurs méthodes de communication. La cible peut être contactée par téléphone ou par mail. Pour entrer en contact avec ses cibles, les pirates n’ont qu’à piocher dans les innombrables fuites de données de ces dernières années. En agrégeant des répertoires compromis issus du dark web, les pirates peuvent à la fois débusquer des moyens de contacter les Français, mais aussi des informations complémentaires pour rendre l’escroquerie plus crédible.
À lire aussi : Une cyberattaque « sophistiquée » frappe un pôle ministériel, des « mesures particulières » ont été prises
« Des fonds en attente »
Pour attirer l’attention de leurs victimes, les escrocs prétextent « des fonds en attente à la Caisse des Dépôts à la suite d’investissements ». Les pirates affirment que de l’argent est disponible au nom de la victime. Pour rendre leur discours crédible, les fraudeurs s’appuient sur une loi de 2014.
Elle oblige les banques et assureurs à transférer à la Caisse des Dépôts les fonds des comptes inactifs, c’est-à-dire les comptes-titres, PEA, assurances-vie ou plans d’épargne dont le titulaire ne s’est plus manifesté depuis plusieurs années. Concrètement, un compte-titres ou un PEA est transféré à la CDC 10 ans après la dernière opération du client. L’institution conserve ensuite ces sommes d’argent pendant 20 ans dans l’attente qu’un bénéficiaire les réclame. Sur le papier, la démarche paraît logique.
C’est là que le piège se referme. Les pirates demandent à la cible « de verser des frais de dossier pour percevoir les fonds en question ». Sans un versement, la victime ne serait pas en mesure de récupérer l’argent consigné à son intention par la Caisse des Dépôts. Cette exigence permet de déceler qu’il s’agit une arnaque. Si des fonds vous sont réellement dus, aucune institution légitime n’exige de payer pour les récupérer. En fait, elle va simplement prélever les frais sur les fonds qui seront reversés à la personne concernée. Le vrai service de la CDC pour récupérer de l’argent, intitulé Ciclade, est entièrement gratuit et accessible en ligne sans aucun frais préalable.
Dans son avertissement, la Caisse des Dépôts précise bien qu’il faut ignorer les mails, les messages ou les appels de ce genre. Si vous « recevez un appel ou un mail de ce type, n’y donnez pas suite », indique l’organisme. L’institution ajoute que « la Caisse des Dépôts ne contacte jamais ses clients de cette manière ».

articles.title: Hackers Start Exploiting Critical Langflow Vulnerability
articles.text:
Threat actors have started exploiting a critical-severity remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in the AI low-code platform Langflow, vulnerability intelligence firm VulnCheck warns.
Tracked as CVE-2026-0768 (CVSS score of 9.8), the security defect exists within the code validator in Langflow’s custom component editor.
Because a user-supplied string is not properly validated before it is used for Python code execution, an attacker could exploit the bug to execute arbitrary code as root without authentication.
The security flaw was reported through ZDI in July 2025 and was publicly disclosed as a zero-day in January 2026. All Langflow releases up to version 1.4.2 are affected.
According to VulnCheck, threat actors have been exploiting the vulnerability to perform reconnaissance and credential harvesting operations.
The cybersecurity firm observed queries for environment variables, secret keys, and SSH access, mainly originating from Russia. By Monday, VulnCheck had seen over 360 exploitation attempts hitting its canaries in the UK.
CVE-2026-0768’s in-the-wild exploitation does not come as a surprise. Last week, VulnCheck warned of a recently observed increase in Langflow vulnerability targeting.
“Before 2026, evidence showed only one Langflow vulnerability known to be exploited in the wild. In 2026, things have changed fast. We’ve now seen 11 additional vulnerabilities targeted and reported as exploited in the wild, highlighting increasing attacker interest in Langflow,” the company said.
VulnCheck has seen more than 15,000 attacks successfully exploiting Langflow instances vulnerable to three of the known exploited flaws, namely CVE-2026-0769, CVE-2025-3248, and CVE-2026-5027.
